extracted.intended_audience: literate London coffee-house readers; genteel public interested in manners, theatre, and current affairs (readers of The Tatler)
extracted.subtask_description: A short early-18th-century periodical essay addressing social behaviour, conversation, theatre (puppet-shows), and contemporary news—aimed at instructing and amusing a polite readership. The page blends reportage, moral observation, theatrical critique, and literary commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good conversation / mutual goodwill
rubrics_metrics.description: "conversation is composed of an assembly of men, as they are men, and not as they are distinguished by fortune...mutual goodwill...the natural, and not the acquired man, is the companion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning, wit, gallantry, and good breeding are 'all but subordinate qualities in society, and are of no value, but as they are subservient to benevolence, and tend to a certain manner of being or appearing equal to the rest of the company.' The essence of conversation is mutual goodwill; desire of superiority contradicts true sociability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a good companion
rubrics_metrics.description: "Florio... never interrupted any man living when he was speaking, or ever ceased to speak, but others lamented that he had done...His discourse ever arises from a fulness of the matter before him, and not from ostentation...forbearance of calumny or bitterness, is owing rather to his good nature than his discretion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good companion: does not interrupt, speaks from substance not ostentation, refrains from calumny and bitterness out of good nature, and displays a general goodwill to mankind. Such qualities make a person 'perfectly qualified for conversation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the natural man to the acquired
rubrics_metrics.description: "the natural, and not the acquired man, is the companion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural simplicity and sincere benevolence are preferred over affected accomplishments; acquired learning/wit/gallantry are valuable only insofar as they support a genuine sociable temper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing types of company (Merry Fellows)
rubrics_metrics.description: "a Merry Fellow is the Saddest Fellow in the world."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boisterous mirth rooted in physical strength and activity (rather than wit or good sense) is presented as inferior company; the observation functions as a social diagnostic—external gaiety may mask melancholy or shallowness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of puppet-plays as dramatic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: "plays represented by puppets are permitted in our universities...and that sort of drama is not wholly thought unworthy the critic of learned heads."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puppet-shows are a legitimate object of learned criticism; one may treat them as a form of dramatic poetry deserving analysis (chronology, decorum, transitions), and even deduce antiquity from form (e.g., single-reciter tradition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Puppet drama: decorum and natural transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: "In its natural transitions, from mournful to merry; as, from the hanging of a lover, to dancing upon the rope...you may discover such a decorum, as is not to be found elsewhere than in our tragi-comedies."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating puppet drama, attend to the naturalness of emotional transitions (mourning to mirth), the maintenance of decorum within those shifts, and structural features (single reciter, burlesque elements) that link it to broader dramatic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indecency in comic/satirical characters (Punch)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A young gentleman...was enraged when Punchinello disturbed a soft love-scene with his ribaldry...you would oblige us mightily by laying down some rules for adjusting the extravagant behaviour of this Almanzor of the play..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical or comic figures (e.g., Punch) should be regulated so their ribaldry does not produce indecencies—especially towards women—if the goal is to retain audience respect and decorum; critics are asked to propose balancing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid transparently mechanical theatrical devices
rubrics_metrics.description: "the world is grown too wise, and can look through these thin devices...He has pretended to write to me also from the Bath...these smart civilities will never run down men of learning...I know well enough your design is to have all men automata, like your puppets."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theatrical or satirical techniques that rely on obvious mechanical tricks or transparent artifice will fail on a discerning audience; effective satire should not reduce people to mere automata or rely on crude devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of postscript to supply omitted material
rubrics_metrics.description: "it being the nature of a postscript to contain something very material which was forgotten, or not clearly expressed in the letter itself...a postscript seems to me the more just way of apology; because otherwise a man makes an excuse before the offence is committed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing, prefer a postscript to supply materially important omitted points (or to apologize after the fact) rather than a preface that apologizes before the offence; stylistic choice illustrated by the 'Brussels Postscript' example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity: do not write without discovering your meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: "to write without discovering your meaning, bears a just resemblance to marching without beat of drum."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing should make the author's meaning evident; failing to express meaning renders the work aimless or absurd—if essential meaning is missing in the main text, supply it via preface/postscript or clarify within the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replies and satire should stick close to the original words
rubrics_metrics.description: "be sure you stick close to my words; for if you bring me into discourses concerning the government of your puppets, I must tell you, I neither am, nor have been, nor will be, at leisure to answer you."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing replies to satire or critique, remain focused on the original words/points; diverting the exchange into unrelated meta-arguments (e.g., about puppet-government) may foreclose engagement and weaken the disputation.
